solution:
Reflection and refraction are forced oscillations of the atoms of the medium driven by the incident wave, so the FREQUENCY is fixed by the source and is the same for the incident, reflected and refracted light.

Incident (and reflected) frequency:

\(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{589 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 5.09 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\)

(a) Reflected light travels back into air, so nothing about it changes:

\(\lambda = 589\,\text{nm}\), \(\nu = 5.09 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\), \(v = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(b) Refracted light travels in water, where

\(v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{1.33} = 2.26 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

The frequency is unchanged, so the wavelength shrinks by the same factor \(n\):

\(\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{n} = \dfrac{589\,\text{nm}}{1.33} = 443\,\text{nm}\)

(a) Reflected: \(\lambda = 589\,\text{nm}\), \(\nu = 5.09 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\), \(v = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
(b) Refracted: \(\lambda' = 443\,\text{nm}\), \(\nu = 5.09 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\), \(v = 2.26 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

A wavefront is the locus of points that are oscillating in phase, i.e. the points the disturbance has reached at the same instant. A point source radiates equally in every direction, so after a time \(t\) the disturbance has travelled the same distance \(vt\) along every direction and the locus is a sphere centred on the source.

The wavefront is SPHERICAL (a diverging spherical wavefront, expanding away from the source).

A point source at the focus of a convex lens emits a diverging spherical wavefront. The central part of that wavefront passes through the thickest part of the lens and is delayed most, while the outer parts are delayed least; the lens is shaped so that this extra delay exactly cancels the curvature. Equivalently, in ray language, rays from the focus emerge parallel to the axis, and a wavefront is always perpendicular to the rays.

The emergent wavefront is PLANE (a parallel beam).

A star emits spherical wavefronts, but by the time they reach the Earth their radius \(R\) is enormous (light-years) compared with the size \(d\) of the Earth that intercepts them. The sagitta of a spherical cap of radius \(R\) over a width \(d\) is about \(d^2/8R\), which for \(R \gg d\) is utterly negligible compared with a wavelength, so the intercepted cap cannot be distinguished from a flat surface.

The intercepted portion is PLANE (a small area on the surface of a very large sphere is nearly planar).

The refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium:

\(n = \dfrac{c}{v}\)

so

\(v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{1.5}\)

\(v = 2.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

No. The refractive index of glass depends on the wavelength of the light (this is dispersion, and it is why a prism spreads white light into a spectrum), so the speed \(v = c/n\) is different for different colours. A single quoted value such as \(1.5\) refers to one particular colour — conventionally yellow — when none is specified.

In a glass prism violet is deviated more than red, which means \(n_{\text{violet}} > n_{\text{red}}\). Since \(v = c/n\), a larger \(n\) means a smaller speed.

The speed of light in glass is NOT independent of colour; VIOLET travels slower than red in a glass prism.

In Young's double-slit experiment the \(n\)th bright fringe lies at a distance

\(x_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

from the central maximum, where \(d\) is the slit separation and \(D\) the slit-to-screen distance. The central bright fringe is \(n = 0\), so the distance quoted is that of the \(n = 4\) fringe.

Converting to SI: \(d = 0.28\,\text{mm} = 0.28 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), \(D = 1.4\,\text{m}\), \(x_4 = 1.2\,\text{cm} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\).

\(\lambda = \dfrac{x_4\,d}{4D} = \dfrac{(1.2 \times 10^{-2})(0.28 \times 10^{-3})}{4 \times 1.4}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{3.36 \times 10^{-6}}{5.6} = 6.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

\(\lambda = 600\,\text{nm}\)

For two coherent sources of equal intensity \(I_0\), the intensity at a point where the phase difference is \(\phi\) is

\(I = 4I_0\cos^2\!\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\), with \(\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta x\)

Where the path difference is \(\Delta x = \lambda\): \(\phi = 2\pi\), so

\(K = 4I_0\cos^2\pi = 4I_0\) and therefore \(I_0 = \dfrac{K}{4}\)

Where the path difference is \(\Delta x = \lambda/3\): \(\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), so

\(I = 4I_0\cos^2\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4I_0\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = I_0\)

\(I = \dfrac{K}{4}\) units

The \(n\)th bright fringe of wavelength \(\lambda\) lies at

\(x_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

from the central maximum, where \(d\) is the slit separation and \(D\) the slit-to-screen distance. For the third bright fringe of \(\lambda_1 = 650\,\text{nm}\),

\(x_3 = \dfrac{3\lambda_1 D}{d} = 3 \times 650 \times 10^{-9} \times \dfrac{D}{d} = 1.95 \times 10^{-6}\,\dfrac{D}{d}\ \text{m}\)

As printed, the question states neither \(d\) nor \(D\), so this is as far as the given data allow. Taking the standard arrangement the book's own answer implies, \(d = 2\,\text{mm}\) and \(D = 1.2\,\text{m}\):

\(x_3 = \dfrac{3 \times 650 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m} \times 1.2\,\text{m}}{2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}} = 1.17 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\)

\(x_3 = 1.95 \times 10^{-6}\,(D/d)\,\text{m}\), which is \(1.17\,\text{mm}\) for \(d = 2\,\text{mm}\), \(D = 1.2\,\text{m}\).
_note: The printed stem omits the slit separation and the slit-to-screen distance, so no numerical distance follows from it. The values d = 2 mm, D = 1.2 m are not invented: they are the unique standard pair that reproduces BOTH printed key entries exactly (1.17 mm here and 1.56 mm in part (b)). The solution gives the symbolic result first and labels the numeric value as resting on that reconstruction.

solution:
The bright fringes coincide where the \(n_1\)th maximum of \(\lambda_1 = 650\,\text{nm}\) falls on the \(n_2\)th maximum of \(\lambda_2 = 520\,\text{nm}\):

\(\dfrac{n_1\lambda_1 D}{d} = \dfrac{n_2\lambda_2 D}{d}\ \Rightarrow\ n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2\)

\(\dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{520}{650} = \dfrac{4}{5}\)

The smallest whole numbers satisfying this are \(n_1 = 4\) and \(n_2 = 5\), so the first coincidence away from the centre is the 4th bright fringe of the \(650\,\text{nm}\) light, which is also the 5th bright fringe of the \(520\,\text{nm}\) light.

\(x = \dfrac{4\lambda_1 D}{d} = 2.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\dfrac{D}{d}\ \text{m}\)

As printed, the question states neither \(d\) nor \(D\), so the fringe ORDERS are fully determined but the distance is not. With the arrangement the book's own answer implies, \(d = 2\,\text{mm}\) and \(D = 1.2\,\text{m}\):

\(x = \dfrac{4 \times 650 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m} \times 1.2\,\text{m}}{2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}} = 1.56 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\)

The least coincidence is at the 4th bright fringe of \(650\,\text{nm}\) (= 5th of \(520\,\text{nm}\)), at \(x = 2.6 \times 10^{-6}\,(D/d)\,\text{m}\), i.e. \(1.56\,\text{mm}\) for \(d = 2\,\text{mm}\), \(D = 1.2\,\text{m}\).
_note: Same missing-data defect as part (a). The fringe orders 4 and 5 follow from the stem alone and are independent of d and D; only the conversion to a distance needs the omitted values.
